pedagogy.summary: Rounding a two-decimal-place number extends 'nearest' to a chosen precision: to the nearest whole, decide between the two neighbouring wholes; to one decimal place, decide between the two neighbouring tenths. The digit ONE place to the right of the target place is the decider. Two traps carry the topic: double rounding (3.47 → 3.5 → 4 when the true nearest whole is 3) and the boundary carry (12.95 to 1dp → 13.0, where the rounded-up tenth ripples into the whole). Rounding is the everyday tool for ESTIMATION (4.83 + 2.17 ≈ 5 + 2 = 7).
bestPractices: Round in ONE step from the original number — never round an already-rounded value; to the nearest whole, only the tenths digit decides (3.47 has 4 tenths, so it rounds to 3)
Identify the single deciding digit: the one immediately to the right of the place you are rounding to
Handle the carry explicitly on a number line: 12.95 lies between 12.9 and 13.0 and is nearer 13.0, so the whole number changes
Keep the target place value: rounding 3.47 to 1dp gives 3.5, and 12.95 to 1dp is written 13.0, not 13
Use rounding to estimate and sense-check (4.83 + 2.17 ≈ 7), and judge whether the estimate is above or below
keyRepresentations: Number line zoomed to the target precision (wholes; then tenths)
Place-value chart marking the target place and the deciding digit
Estimation on a number line for sums like 4.83 + 2.17
Boundary number line 12.9–13.0 for the carry case
commonMisconceptions: Double rounding: 3.47 → 3.5 → 4 to the nearest whole
Uses the wrong deciding digit — looks at the hundredths (or a chain of digits) when rounding to a whole
Drops the boundary carry: 12.95 → 12.10 or 12.9 instead of 13.0
Omits the trailing zero / place: writes 13 when 1dp is asked, or truncates

learn.summary: Teaches rounding two-decimal-place numbers to the nearest whole and to one decimal place, treating rounding as choosing between two neighbouring values at a chosen precision, decided by the single digit immediately to the right of the target place. Two central traps: double rounding (3.47 → 3.5 → 4 when the nearest whole is 3) and the boundary carry (12.95 to 1dp → 13.0, where the rounded tenth ripples into the whole). Rounding is linked to estimation (4.83 + 2.17 ≈ 5 + 2 = 7); for this particular pair the rounding errors cancel, so the estimate equals the true sum. A zoomable number line is the lead activity because the same number can be rounded to different precisions and the carry can be watched; a set of checkable questions, a static annotated line, and diagnostic prompts are preserved as complementary tools.

activities.title: Zoomable number line: one-step rounding and the visible carry
feedback: If a learner reaches 4 for 3.47 to the nearest whole via 3.5, show on the line that 3.47 never reaches 3.5; round once, straight from the original, and only the tenths digit (4) counts.

If a learner writes 12.9 for 12.95 to 1dp, show on the 12.9–13.0 line that 12.95 sits exactly halfway between 12.9 and 13.0, and that the usual rule (a deciding digit of 5 rounds up) gives 13.0; when the tenth rounds up past 9 it carries into the whole, just like 9 + 1 in whole-number columns.
Reinforce keeping the target place: 12.95 to 1dp is written 13.0, not 13.

For the estimate, accept 'exactly equal': rounding 4.83 up by 0.17 and 2.17 down by 0.17 cancels, so 7 is neither above nor below 7.00 for this pair — a good moment to see that rounding errors can offset.
activities.rationale: A number line that can be re-zoomed lets the same number be rounded to different precisions so the deciding digit changes visibly, and the 12.95 carry can be watched rather than asserted. The optional zoom control, the midpoint marking, the side-by-side wrong-path comparison, and the 'ticking up' animation make the mechanism concrete; these are illustrative, not mandatory. Source guidance frames rounding as choosing between a just-greater and just-less number located on a number line, and warns that applying a procedure without this awareness produces cascading/double rounding and boundary-carry (trail-of-9s) errors.
sourceClaims: Rounding to a chosen precision is 'choosing between two numbers, one just greater and one just less', decided by locating the number on a number line; 'memorising and applying a procedure... without this overall awareness often results in errors', including sequential/cascading rounding up (rounding an already-rounded value rather than in one step) and the 'trail of 9s' boundary carry (e.g. 9999 rounds to 10000), where a rounded digit ripples into the next place.
Year 5 pupils are taught to 'round decimals with 2 decimal places to the nearest whole number and to 1 decimal place' (verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: Plot 3.47 on a number line showing whole numbers 3 and 4; mark the 3.5 midpoint and judge that 3.47 sits just below it, so it is nearer 3.

Deliberately try the tempting wrong path: round 3.47 to 3.5 first, then watch 3.5 round up to 4 — the WRONG whole. Compare side by side with going straight from 3.47 (tenths digit 4, below half) which gives 3.
Zoom the line to tenths and round 3.47 to one decimal place (3.5).

Switch to a 12.9–13.0 view and round 12.95 to one decimal place; notice it sits exactly halfway, so by the usual rule (a deciding 5 rounds up) it snaps to 13.0, and watch the whole-number digit tick from 12 to 13 as the carry ripples in.

Use an estimation view to round 4.83 and 2.17 each to the nearest whole and add (5 + 2 = 7); then compare with the true sum (7.00) and say whether the estimate is above, below, or exactly equal — here rounding 4.83 up and 2.17 down cancel, so the estimate equals the true total.
activities.intendedInsight: Round in ONE step from the original number; to the nearest whole only the tenths digit decides, so 3.47 → 3. The boundary carry (12.95 → 13.0) is a real event where a rounded-up tenth ripples into the whole, not a rule failure.

activities.title: Identify the deciding digit on a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner rounds 3.47 to a whole using the 7 (→ 4), re-establish the target place and show the single digit to its right is the only decider; have them point to it first.
If a learner rounds up 'because there are digits after', clarify that only that one deciding digit matters, not the presence of further digits.
activities.rationale: Explicitly locating the target place and its single deciding digit targets the wrong-deciding-digit misconception. A static or tap-to-reveal chart serves as a reference aid; it labels the deciding digit for one case but does not itself animate precision-switching or the carry, so it supports rather than replaces the number-line activity.
learnerActions: Place a number such as 3.47 in a place-value chart and name the place you are rounding to.
Point to the ONE digit immediately to the right of that place as the sole decider before rounding — for rounding to a whole, the tenths digit (4); for rounding to 1dp, the hundredths digit.
Explain why the 7 (hundredths) does NOT decide the nearest whole of 3.47.
activities.intendedInsight: The deciding digit is exactly the one place to the right of the target place (the tenths when rounding to a whole, the hundredths when rounding to 1dp) — never a chain of digits.

activities.title: Checkable rounding and estimation questions
feedback: Answer 4 for 3.47 to the nearest whole signals double rounding — revisit the one-step number-line comparison.
Answer 12.9 for 12.95 to 1dp signals a dropped carry; 12.10 signals a mishandled carry — revisit the 12.9–13.0 line.
Answer 13 (without the .0) signals a lost trailing place — the question asked for 1dp, so write 13.0.
For the estimate, 'exactly equal' is correct here: the +0.17 and −0.17 rounding errors cancel, so accept it rather than requiring above/below.
activities.rationale: Rounding to a stated precision and estimation are cleanly checkable, and targeted distractors (4 from double rounding, 12.9 from a dropped carry, 13 from a lost place) surface specific misconceptions. This checkable format is well suited to practising and checking the procedure and surfacing these specific errors; it does not itself animate the precision-switching or carry that the number line makes visible, so it works best following the number-line work.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils are taught to 'round decimals with 2 decimal places to the nearest whole number and to 1 decimal place' (verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number (answer 3).

Estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding each to the nearest whole (5 + 2 = 7) and say whether the estimate is above, below, or exactly equal to the true total (7.00) — for this pair the rounding errors cancel, so it is exactly equal.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner can round correctly to a stated precision in one step and use rounding to estimate and sense-check a sum.

activities.title: Diagnostic sequence and probing questions
feedback: 3.47 to the nearest whole is the double-rounding hinge: a secure learner reads the tenths (4 < 5) and says 3 in one step; a double-rounder gets 3.5 then 4.
12.95 to 1dp is the carry hinge: secure → 13.0; dropped carry → 12.9; wrong carry → 12.10.

For the estimate, accept 'exactly equal' as the correct relationship for 4.83 + 2.17: the rounding errors (+0.17 and −0.17) offset exactly, so the estimate 7 equals the true sum 7.00 — do not require above/below.
Finish by asking the learner to transfer the method to a new two-decimal-place number.
activities.rationale: These prompts come directly from the assessment design and separate the three error patterns (double rounding, carry-handling, truncation) while requiring the learner to articulate reasoning, supporting transfer to a new number. The estimate relationship is left open in the prompt so it genuinely diagnoses the learner's reasoning, with the 'errors cancel' explanation reserved for feedback.
learnerActions: Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number, then round 3.47 to one decimal place; say which single digit tells you each answer and why not the 7.
Round 12.95 to one decimal place and explain what happens to the whole-number part and why.
Estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding each to the nearest whole; then say whether the estimate is above, below, or exactly equal to the real total.
If you said 3.5 and then 4 for the nearest whole, redo it going straight from 3.47 — which whole is it actually nearer?
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining the deciding digit and the carry, in one step from the original, distinguishes secure rounding from double rounding, dropped/mishandled carry, and truncation.

constraints: Round in ONE step from the original number — never round an already-rounded value.
Keep the target place value: rounding to 1dp requires the trailing place (write 13.0, not 13).
The static annotated number line and place-value chart are reference/scaffold aids: they can label the deciding digit for one case but do not demonstrate precision-switching or the carry dynamically.

The set of checkable questions checks answers and surfaces misconceptions via distractors; this format does not itself animate the precision-switching or carry that the number line shows, so pair it with the number-line work rather than treating it as the sole route to the nearness concept.
For the estimation example 4.83 + 2.17, the estimate (7) equals the true sum (7.00); do not require learners to pick 'above' or 'below' — accept 'exactly equal'.
Prerequisite reteach for double rounding and wrong-deciding-digit errors is flagged to an earlier place-value micro-topic in the source assessment.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Original-row error corrected: the assessment's probe 'estimate 4.83 + 2.17 — is your estimate above or below the real total?' has no above/below answer, because rounding 4.83 up (+0.17) and 2.17 down (−0.17) cancel, giving estimate 7 = true 7.00. All learner-facing actions now allow 'exactly equal'; the diagnostic prompt is left open with the explanation in feedback. The original binary phrasing is noted here and in preservationAudit.uncertain, not reproduced as a required answer.

Arithmetic/logic self-audit: 3.47 to nearest whole = 3 (tenths 4 < 5), to 1dp = 3.5 (hundredths 7 ≥ 5); 12.95 to 1dp = 13.0 (carry correct); 4.83 → 5, 2.17 → 2, estimate 7 vs true 7.00 (equal). Distractors '4' (3.47) and '12.9'/'12.10'/'13' (12.95) are intentional wrong options and must never be presented as correct.

The source's 'poor fit' claims that depth 'adds nothing' and that a mechanical procedure offers no worthwhile dialogue are catalog preferences, not established pedagogical laws; omitted from learner-facing guidance rather than asserted as universal.

The source 'possible' claim that a static line 'cannot show precision-switching or the carry dynamically' is retained narrowly as a scaffold limitation, not as a claim that static images cannot teach.
Catalog artefact vocabulary ('quiz') was replaced with neutral descriptions ('set of checkable questions') in the summary and constraints.

probeDeeper: To round 3.47 to the nearest whole, which single digit tells you the answer — and why not the 7?
You said 3.5 and then 4 — what do you get going straight from 3.47? Which whole is it actually nearer?
Round 12.95 to one decimal place — what happens to the whole-number part, and why?
Estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding each — is your estimate above or below the real total?
assess.correctAnswer: 3.47 → 3 (nearest whole; tenths digit is 4) and 3.5 (to 1dp); 12.95 → 13.0 (to 1dp, the carry ripples into the whole); 4.83 + 2.17 ≈ 5 + 2 = 7.

errorPatterns.pattern: Double rounding: rounds 3.47 to 3.5 first, then rounds 3.5 up to 4 for the nearest whole
errorPatterns.nextMove: Round once, straight from the original: to the nearest whole only the tenths digit (4) counts, so 3.47 → 3. Show on the line it never reaches 3.5.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 4 for 3.47 to the nearest whole, and explains it by first getting 3.5

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops or mishandles the boundary carry: 12.95 → 1dp gives 12.9 or 12.10 instead of 13.0
errorPatterns.nextMove: On a 12.9–13.0 line, show 12.95 is nearer 13.0; when the tenth rounds up past 9 it carries into the whole, just like 9 + 1 in whole-number columns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounds the tenths up but leaves the whole unchanged (12.9), or writes an impossible 12.10

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the wrong deciding digit — looks at the hundredths (7) when rounding 3.47 to a whole, or rounds up because 'there are digits after'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Identify the place being rounded to and the ONE digit immediately to its right as the sole decider; practise pointing to it before rounding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounds 3.47 to a whole by the 7 (→ 4), or cannot say which single digit decides

responseLevels.gap: Truncates or rounds by the wrong digit; cannot round to a stated precision.
responseLevels.full: Rounds to the nearest whole and to 1dp in ONE step from the original, handles the 12.95 → 13.0 carry, uses rounding to estimate 4.83 + 2.17 ≈ 7, explains which digit decides at each precision, and transfers to a new number.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds correctly to one precision but double-rounds when finding the nearest whole, or mishandles the 12.95 carry, or drops the trailing .0.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number, and then round 3.47 to one decimal place. Next, round 12.95 to one decimal place. Finally, estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding.' Watch each step — especially whether they go via 3.5 for the whole, and what happens to 12.95.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 3.47 to the nearest whole is the double-rounding hinge: a secure child reads the tenths (4 < 5) and says 3 in one step; a double-rounder rounds to 3.5 first, then up to 4 — a different, wrong answer. 12.95 to 1dp is the carry hinge: a secure child gets 13.0, while others write 12.9 (ignored the carry) or 12.10 (carried wrongly). Together they separate double rounding, carry-handling, and truncation.
